traditions.name: Reynolds Club Seal
traditions.description: Legend says a student who steps on the University seal in the lobby of the Reynolds Club won't graduate in four years. Visitors can see the seal in the student union lobby and decide whether to test the myth.

traditions.name: Cobb Gate Gargoyles
traditions.description: By campus lore, the grotesques on Cobb Gate stand for the admissions officers and the climb of first- to fourth-year students, with the fourth-year at the top. Visitors can walk through the gate and look up to spot each figure.

traditions.name: Botany Pond
traditions.description: Botany Pond in Hull Court is a beloved campus spot where visitors come to see the ducklings and turtles. Stop by the pond for a quiet look at the wildlife and gardens.

traditions.name: Rockefeller Chapel Carillon
traditions.description: The 72-bell carillon at the top of Rockefeller Chapel is played in a daily recital, and student guild members give weekly concerts with bell-tower tours beforehand for anyone interested. Visitors can listen from the quad or join a tour.

details.airportInfo: Midway is the closer of Chicago's two airports to Hyde Park, on the city's South Side. O'Hare International (ORD) handles far more long-haul flights but is a longer trip across the city.
details.funFact: The campus mixes two big ideas: Gothic quadrangles and some of the boldest modern buildings in America, from Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House to Helmut Jahn's glass-domed Mansueto Library.
details.languageInfo: Campus has its own shorthand: the Regenstein Library is simply 'the Reg', and the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures was known for a century as the Oriental Institute.
details.transportationFact: The main quadrangles are compact enough to walk. Metra Electric trains run between Hyde Park and downtown Chicago, and university shuttles loop the neighborhood.

buildings.name: Rockefeller Chapel
buildings.description: Bertram Goodhue's soaring Collegiate Gothic chapel was built between 1925 and 1928 without structural steel. Around 70 sculptures are carved into its stone, and its carillon tower is, by covenant, the tallest building on campus.

buildings.name: Robie House
buildings.description: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie-style masterpiece hugs the ground with long brick bands and roofs cantilevered far out over its terraces. Completed in 1910, it helped popularize picture windows and attached garages in American homes.

buildings.name: Regenstein Library
buildings.description: 'The Reg' is the university's main library and one of its great Brutalist statements, designed by Walter Netsch of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. It opened in 1970 and holds one of the largest collections of books in the world.

buildings.name: Mansueto Library
buildings.description: Helmut Jahn's elliptical glass dome sits right beside the Regenstein. Readers work under the glass while millions of volumes are stored in stacks fifty feet underground, fetched by robotic cranes in about three minutes.

buildings.wiki: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures
buildings.name: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures
buildings.description: Long known as the Oriental Institute, this Gothic Revival building was dedicated in 1931 and carries ancient Near Eastern motifs in its stonework. Inside stand a 40-ton lamassu from Khorsabad and a monumental statue of King Tutankhamun.

buildings.name: Ida Noyes Hall
buildings.description: Built in 1916 as a clubhouse and gymnasium for the university's women, this limestone Neo-Gothic hall is full of fireplaces, ornate plaster ceilings and rich wood paneling.

traditions.name: Main Building Front Steps
traditions.description: Undergraduates avoid the front steps of the Main Building, as legend says using them means not graduating; seniors first walk them at graduation. Visitors are welcome to use the steps and take a photo under the Golden Dome.

traditions.name: Light a Candle at the Grotto
traditions.description: Students, alumni and visitors light candles and say a prayer at the Grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes; Notre Dame Magazine jokes you should leave double the suggested offering "just to be sure." Visitors can light a candle and read Tom Dooley's letter to Father Hesburgh there.

traditions.name: Touchdown Jesus
traditions.description: The Word of Life mural on the face of the Hesburgh Library, better known as Touchdown Jesus, is one of the campus landmarks where visiting families line up for photos. Visitors can pose in front of it by the reflecting pool.

traditions.name: Fair Catch Corby
traditions.description: The statue of Father William Corby with his arm raised, nicknamed Fair-Catch Corby, stands outside Corby Hall and is a classic campus photo stop. Visitors can pose beside it.

traditions.name: Lyons Hall Arch
traditions.description: Campus superstition holds that a couple who kiss under the archway of Lyons Hall may get engaged before graduation. Visitors can walk through the arch and see it for themselves.

details.airportInfo: South Bend International is a short drive from campus. The South Shore Line commuter train runs from the airport to downtown Chicago.
details.funFact: The Golden Dome, topped by a statue of Mary, rises over a campus of around 170 buildings set around two lakes and seven quadrangles, often ranked among the most beautiful in the world.
details.languageInfo: Campus has its own vocabulary: the Main Quad is 'God Quad', and the Word of Life mural on the Hesburgh Library is better known as 'Touchdown Jesus'.
details.transportationFact: The historic core around the Main Quad and South Quad is best explored on foot, with the Basilica, the Dome and the Grotto all a few minutes apart.

buildings.name: Main Building (Golden Dome)
buildings.description: After fire destroyed its predecessor in 1879, this Second Empire landmark was raised again in a single summer. Its Golden Dome, crowned by a statue of Mary, is the university's most recognizable sight.

buildings.wiki: Basilica of the Sacred Heart (Notre Dame)
buildings.name: Basilica of the Sacred Heart
buildings.description: This Gothic Revival church glows with 44 large stained glass windows and murals painted over 17 years by the Vatican painter Luigi Gregori. Its 70-metre bell tower makes it the tallest university chapel in America.
buildings.architect: Edward Sorin, Alexis Granger and Brother Charles Harding

buildings.name: Hesburgh Library
buildings.description: Opened in 1963, the library's 64-metre stone tower faces the football stadium with the giant Word of Life mural, known to everyone as 'Touchdown Jesus'. Its narrow, nearly windowless 13-story tower rises from a wider two-story base of glass, brick and granite.
buildings.address: Hesburgh Library Quad, Notre Dame, IN 46556

buildings.name: Sorin Hall
buildings.description: The oldest residence hall at Notre Dame, built in 1889, is a Châteauesque building just south of the Basilica. Its famous front porch was added in 1905.
buildings.architect: Willoughby J. Edbrooke and Franklin Pierce Burnham

buildings.name: Alumni Hall
buildings.description: Maginnis & Walsh built this Collegiate Gothic residence hall on South Quad in 1931. It has a richly decorated neo-Gothic chapel, and a statue known as 'Joe College' looks out from its south side.

buildings.name: Walsh Family Hall of Architecture
buildings.description: Home of a school famous for teaching classical design, this 2019 building by John Simpson has a Hall of Casts, a stoa, a tower and a courtyard. It won the 2019 Acanthus Award for institutional architecture.

traditions.name: The Block M on the Diag
traditions.description: Superstition says stepping on the bronze M in the Diag before your first exam means you'll fail it, so students walk around it. Visitors can find the M at the centre of the Diag and take a photo beside it.

traditions.name: Engineering Arch
traditions.description: Legend says a couple who kiss under the West Hall engineering arch at midnight will eventually marry. Visitors can walk through the arch at the southeast corner of the Diag.

traditions.name: The Cube
traditions.description: Endover, a 15-foot steel cube balanced on one corner in Regents' Plaza, is mounted so that it spins with a push. Visitors can give it a spin.

traditions.name: The Rock
traditions.description: A large boulder at Hill Street and Washtenaw Avenue has been painted over and over since the 1950s by students and the public. Visitors can stop to see its latest coat of paint.

details.airportInfo: Detroit Metro is about a half-hour drive east of Ann Arbor and is the main airport for the region.
details.funFact: Detroit architect Albert Kahn shaped Michigan's Central Campus, designing Hill Auditorium, Angell Hall, the Clements Library and Burton Memorial Tower.
details.languageInfo: The school colors are maize and blue, and the teams are the Wolverines.
details.transportationFact: Central Campus is walkable. The university's free Blue Buses link Central, North and medical campuses.

buildings.name: Burton Memorial Tower
buildings.description: Albert Kahn's 1936 clock tower blends Art Deco and Art Moderne in a reinforced concrete shell faced with limestone. It holds a grand carillon of 53 bells weighing 43 tons, among the heaviest in the world.
buildings.address: 230 N Ingalls St, Ann Arbor, MI 48109

buildings.name: William L. Clements Library
buildings.description: Albert Kahn modeled this 1923 rare book library in the Italian Renaissance style on Vignola's casino at the Villa Farnese. It guards a remarkable collection of early American books, maps and manuscripts.
buildings.address: South University Ave, Ann Arbor, MI 48109

buildings.name: Detroit Observatory
buildings.description: Completed in 1854 on a hill above the Huron River, this was the university's first scientific research building and one of the oldest observatories of its kind in the nation. Its dome once held the third-largest refracting telescope in the world.
buildings.address: Observatory St and Ann St, Ann Arbor, MI 48109

buildings.name: Martha Cook Building
buildings.description: York and Sawyer designed this Collegiate Gothic residence, opened in 1915 as the first dormitory for women on campus. A statue of Shakespeare's Portia by Furio Piccirilli watches over the entrance.
buildings.address: 906 S University Ave, Ann Arbor, MI 48109

buildings.wiki: University of Michigan Museum of Art
buildings.name: University of Michigan Museum of Art
buildings.description: The museum lives in Alumni Memorial Hall, a neoclassical war memorial completed in 1910, joined since 2009 by a new wing from Brad Cloepfil's Allied Works that more than doubled its size.
buildings.architect: Donaldson and Meier; Allied Works Architecture (2009 wing)
buildings.address: South State St, Ann Arbor, MI 48109

traditions.name: Pumpkin Launch
traditions.description: Every October during family weekend, student teams build catapults and trebuchets and compete to fling pumpkins for distance and accuracy on Ed Glancy Field. The event draws spectators from across Chicago.

traditions.name: S. R. Crown Hall
traditions.description: Crown Hall, home of the College of Architecture, is widely considered Mies van der Rohe's finest work and seems to float above the lawn on travertine steps. Visitors can see this landmark of modern architecture up close.

traditions.name: The Tube over the Campus Center
traditions.description: Rem Koolhaas's McCormick Tribune Campus Center has a stainless-steel tube carrying CTA Green Line trains right over its roof. Visitors can watch trains pass through the tube overhead.

details.airportInfo: Midway, on Chicago's South Side, is the closer of the city's two airports. O'Hare International (ORD) has far more long-haul flights but is a longer trip across the city.
details.funFact: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe directed IIT's architecture school for two decades and designed much of its campus, making it one of the largest collections of his buildings anywhere.
details.languageInfo: Students call the Mies-designed Carr Memorial Chapel the 'God Box', after its plain brick shape.
details.transportation: Walking / CTA Green and Red Lines
details.transportationFact: The CTA Green Line runs straight through campus, wrapped in a stainless steel tube where it passes over the Campus Center, and the Red Line stops just west of campus.

buildings.name: S. R. Crown Hall
buildings.description: Mies van der Rohe's glass-and-steel hall for the architecture school he led is one big open room: the roof hangs from four girders on four pairs of columns, leaving no interior columns at all. It is a National Historic Landmark.

buildings.name: Carr Memorial Chapel
buildings.description: The only religious building Mies van der Rohe ever designed is a simple one-story brick box, finished in 1952. Students nicknamed it the 'God Box'.
buildings.address: Michigan Ave and 32nd St, Chicago, IL 60616

buildings.name: McCormick Tribune Campus Center
buildings.description: Rem Koolhaas's first building in the United States, opened in 2003, traced students' shortcuts across an old parking lot to create its diagonal interior streets. A 530-foot stainless steel tube carries the CTA Green Line over the roof to keep out the noise.

buildings.name: Rowe Village
buildings.description: Helmut Jahn's residence hall, completed in 2003 and first called State Street Village, looks like one long building but is really three, sharing a single facade.

traditions.name: Edgar Allan Poe's Room
traditions.description: Poe's student room at 13 West Range is kept furnished as an 1826 student room. Visitors look in through a glass door and can press a button to hear a recording about Poe's time at UVA.

traditions.name: Painted Beta Bridge
traditions.description: Since the latter half of the 20th century, students have painted messages on the Rugby Road bridge, from club events to birthdays and memorials. Stop by to see what is painted on it this week.

traditions.name: Lighting of the Lawn
traditions.description: Each December, a cappella performances on the Lawn end with a light show on the Rotunda. The lights around the Academical Village then stay lit every night until early January.

traditions.name: Trick-or-Treating on the Lawn
traditions.description: On Halloween, students living in the Lawn rooms hand out candy to local children, a tradition since the 1980s. Families line up along the 54 Lawn rooms.

details.airportInfo: Charlottesville's small regional airport is a short drive north of the university. Larger airports in Richmond and Washington, D.C. are a two- to three-hour drive away.
details.funFact: Thomas Jefferson planned his Academical Village around a library, the Rotunda, instead of a church. Together with his home at Monticello it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
details.languageInfo: At UVA the campus is called 'the Grounds', and the sports teams are the Cavaliers, also known as the Wahoos.
details.transportationFact: Central Grounds around the Lawn is easy to walk. Free University Transit Service buses connect the rest of the Grounds.

buildings.name: The Rotunda
buildings.description: Jefferson modeled his library on the Pantheon in Rome at half its size: the Rotunda is 77 feet in both height and diameter. Fire gutted it in 1895, and Stanford White rebuilt it with a fireproof Guastavino tile dome.

buildings.name: The Lawn
buildings.description: The terraced green heart of Jefferson's Academical Village is framed by ten pavilions, where faculty live upstairs and teach below, linked by colonnades of 54 student rooms. Living on the Lawn in fourth year is one of UVA's highest honors.

buildings.name: Clark Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1932 as the home of the School of Law, this Classical Revival building now holds the Department of Environmental Sciences and a science and engineering library. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

buildings.name: Carr's Hill
buildings.description: The university president's house, built in 1906 by McKim, Mead & White, is a two-story brick house with a tall Doric portico. It looks out over the Academical Village.

traditions.name: Through the Sallyport
traditions.description: By tradition, Rice students pass through the Sallyport arch in Lovett Hall as they leave at graduation and avoid it until then. Stand under the arch and look across the Academic Quad.

traditions.name: Skyspace at Sunset
traditions.description: James Turrell's Twilight Epiphany Skyspace puts on a free light show at sunrise and sunset, as changing colored light transforms the sky seen through its roof opening. Arrive early for a seat.

traditions.name: The Moon Speech Stadium
traditions.description: In 1962 President Kennedy spoke at Rice Stadium and challenged the nation to reach the Moon by the end of the decade. Visit the stadium where the famous speech was given.

traditions.name: The Marching Owl Band
traditions.description: The Marching Owl Band, or MOB, is a scatter band: instead of marching in formation, it performs comic skits at football games. Catch its halftime show.

traditions.name: A Tree for Every Student
traditions.description: More than 4,000 trees and shrubs make the whole campus an arboretum, which gave rise to the legend that Rice has a tree for every student. Stroll the shady quads.

details.airportInfo: Hobby is the closer of Houston's two main airports to Rice. George Bush Intercontinental (IAH) has many more long-haul flights but is a longer drive north.
details.funFact: When Rice opened in 1912, students paid no tuition at all, as founder William Marsh Rice's will and the institute's first charter required.
details.languageInfo: The mascot is Sammy the Owl: when Texas A&M students stole the owl mascot in 1917, a detective's coded telegram reported that 'Sammy is fairly well.' The colors are blue and gray.
details.transportationFact: The wooded campus is easy to walk. The METRORail Red Line runs along Main Street, with the Hermann Park/Rice U station near the campus's eastern corner.

buildings.name: Lovett Hall
buildings.description: Ralph Adams Cram's firm designed Rice's landmark first building, the asymmetrical Administration Building completed in 1912. Graduating students leave the university through its arched Sallyport.

buildings.name: Fondren Library
buildings.description: Houston architect John F. Staub designed Rice's main library, dedicated in 1949 and funded by the family of Humble Oil co-founder Walter Fondren. It was known for its open stacks and Art Deco touches.

buildings.name: Herzstein Hall
buildings.description: Cram, Goodhue & Ferguson designed this 1914 building as Rice's physics hall, one of the first on the Academic Quad. Its amphitheater was the largest on campus when it was built.

buildings.name: Maxfield Hall
buildings.description: Built in 1912 as the Mechanical Laboratory and power house, crowned by a tall campanile, this was the second building on campus. Renovated and renamed Maxfield Hall in 2021, it now houses the statistics department.

buildings.name: Cohen House
buildings.description: William Ward Watkin, Rice's supervising architect, designed this faculty club, completed in 1927 with a gift honoring Robert and Agnes Cohen. It was the first building in Texas built as a university faculty club.

buildings.name: First Community Stadium
buildings.description: Opened in 1950 with 70,000 seats, Rice's football stadium hosted President Kennedy's "We choose to go to the Moon" speech in 1962 and Super Bowl VIII in 1974.
buildings.architect: Hermon Lloyd & W. B. Morgan; Milton McGinty

buildings.name: Tudor Fieldhouse
buildings.description: Opened in 1950 as Rice Gymnasium, this arena was renamed for alumnus Bobby Tudor, who led its renovation. Its court, Autry Court, is home to Owls basketball and volleyball.

buildings.name: Reckling Park
buildings.description: Jackson & Ryan designed the Owls' baseball park, opened in 2000 on the site of Cameron Field. The team that won the 2003 College World Series played its home games here.

buildings.name: Moody Center for the Arts
buildings.description: Los Angeles architect Michael Maltzan designed this arts center, opened in 2017 with studio classrooms, a makerspace and gallery space for visiting artists.

buildings.wiki: Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy
buildings.name: Baker Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1997, Baker Hall houses Rice's Baker Institute for Public Policy, a think tank founded in 1993 and named for former Secretary of State James A. Baker III.

traditions.name: The Gravity Monument
traditions.description: Hidden in the trees off Dowman Drive is a pink marble monument that Roger Babson gave Emory in 1963 to honor the sciences. Many say it looks more like a tombstone in the woods. See if you can find it.

traditions.name: Lullwater Preserve and Tower
traditions.description: Lullwater Preserve is a 154-acre stretch of woods and water that walkers and joggers enjoy. Follow the trail to the old granite tower Walter Candler built beside his dam to power his house.

traditions.name: Words Under the Eaves
traditions.description: Henry Hornbostel set the look of the Quad with pink Georgia marble and red tile roofs. Look up under the eaves of the older buildings to find carved words naming what was once taught inside.

traditions.name: Source Route
traditions.description: Behind the Carlos Museum, a set of stairs leads down into Baker Woodland. It is part of an environmental sculpture installed in the 1970s. Take the steps into the woods.

traditions.name: Robinson Clock Tower Bells
traditions.description: The clock tower on Cox Hall carries carillon bells dedicated in 2001 to honor trustee J. William Robinson and his wife. Listen for them as you cross the campus.

details.airportInfo: Hartsfield–Jackson, south of downtown Atlanta, is the nearest airport. Emory's Druid Hills campus is northeast of downtown.
details.funFact: Emory moved to Atlanta from Oxford, Georgia, in 1915 after Coca-Cola founder Asa Griggs Candler gave land and a million dollars. Henry Hornbostel then set the campus look of pink Georgia marble and red tile roofs.
details.languageInfo: The school colors are blue and gold, and the teams are the Eagles. Emory has two mascots: Swoop the Eagle and Dooley the skeleton.
details.transportationFact: The Cliff, Emory's shuttle system, runs routes around campus and to nearby neighborhoods. Its buses run on biodiesel made from recycled cooking oil.

buildings.name: Michael C. Carlos Museum
buildings.description: Michael Graves designed this museum building on the historic Quad, completed in 1993. It holds the largest collection of ancient art in the Southeast, from Egypt, Greece and Rome to Africa and the ancient Americas.

buildings.name: Candler Library
buildings.description: Coca-Cola founder Asa Griggs Candler paid for this library, built in 1926 and renovated in 2004. Inside are the Matheson Reading Room and a 1920s copy of Thorvaldsen's Triumph of Alexander frieze.

buildings.name: Robert W. Woodruff Library
buildings.description: Emory's main library was built in 1969 as a 10-story tower; a four-story wing was added in front in 1995. The Rose Library of rare books and manuscripts is on the tenth floor.

buildings.name: Cannon Chapel
buildings.description: Paul Rudolph designed this chapel for the Candler School of Theology. President Jimmy Carter spoke at its groundbreaking in 1979, and it is named for former dean William R. Cannon.

buildings.name: Rita Anne Rollins Building
buildings.description: Completed in 2008, this home of the Candler School of Theology has marble and stucco walls under a clay tile roof. A 2014 addition links it to the Pitts Theology Library.

buildings.name: Glenn Memorial Church
buildings.description: Built in 1931 near the main entrance to campus, this Methodist church honors minister Wilbur Fisk Glenn. For years Emory held its commencement in the church school amphitheater next door.

buildings.wiki: Donna and Marvin Schwartz Center for Performing Arts
buildings.name: Schwartz Center for Performing Arts
buildings.description: Completed in 2003, this arts center is built around the 825-seat Emerson Concert Hall, a tall shoebox hall modeled on halls like Vienna's Musikverein. Its stucco and Portuguese limestone echo the older campus.
buildings.address: N Decatur Rd at Clifton Rd, Atlanta, GA 30322

buildings.name: Goizueta Business School
buildings.description: Named for Coca-Cola chairman Roberto Goizueta, the business school's building at Fishburne Drive and Clifton Road was dedicated in 1997. A second building for research and doctoral study followed in 2005.
buildings.address: Fishburne Dr at Clifton Rd NE, Atlanta, GA 30322

buildings.name: Emory University Hospital
buildings.description: The hospital moved to the campus in 1922 into a new 275-bed building given by Asa Griggs Candler. Today it is an 853-bed teaching hospital staffed by the faculty of Emory's School of Medicine.

buildings.name: Lullwater House
buildings.description: Ivey and Crook designed this L-shaped mansion for Walter T. Candler, completed in 1926 with granite quarried on the estate. Emory bought it in 1958, and it is now the president's home overlooking Candler Lake.

traditions.name: Ride the St. Charles Streetcar
traditions.description: The St. Charles line has run since 1835 and is the oldest continuously operating streetcar line in the world. Ride it to the Tulane University stop in front of Gibson Hall.

traditions.name: Tiffany Windows on Woodward Way
traditions.description: Two Louis Comfort Tiffany stained-glass triptychs, made in the 1890s for a chapel at Newcomb College's old Garden District campus, now line the Woodward Way breezeway at the Newcomb Art Museum. Stop and look for them.

traditions.name: Rogers Memorial Chapel
traditions.description: More of Tulane's Tiffany stained glass is in the Myra Clare Rogers Memorial Chapel on the Newcomb side of campus. Peek inside to see the windows.

traditions.name: Maya Gallery in Dinwiddie Hall
traditions.description: The Middle American Research Institute has studied the Maya since 1924. Its gallery on the third floor of Dinwiddie Hall is open to the public on weekdays.

details.nickname: Not for Oneself, but for One's Own
details.airportName: Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport
details.airportInfo: Louis Armstrong New Orleans International is in Kenner, about 11 miles (18 km) west of downtown New Orleans.
details.funFact: Tulane's Uptown campus faces Audubon Park across St. Charles Avenue. Gibson Hall, built in 1894, was the first academic building on the campus, and the Newcomb College buildings were designed by Yale architect James Gamble Rogers.
details.languageInfo: The school colors are green and blue, and the teams are the Green Wave. The mascot is Riptide the Pelican.
details.transportationFact: The St. Charles Streetcar stops right in front of the campus and runs to downtown New Orleans. McAlister Place, once a road through the middle of campus, became a walkway in 2009.

buildings.name: Gibson Hall
buildings.description: Built in 1894, Gibson Hall is the oldest building on the Uptown campus and its front door on St. Charles Avenue. Harrod and Andry designed it in Richardsonian Romanesque stone over brick.
buildings.address: 6823 St Charles Ave, New Orleans, LA 70118

buildings.wiki: Tulane University School of Architecture and Built Environment
buildings.name: Richardson Memorial Hall
buildings.description: Built in 1908, this five-story hall on the oldest part of campus is home to the School of Architecture and Built Environment. A major renovation and expansion reopened it in 2025.

buildings.name: Howard-Tilton Memorial Library
buildings.description: Tulane's main library moved into its current building on Freret Street in 1968. It holds the Hogan Jazz Archive and the Latin American Library. Hurricane Katrina flooded its basement, and a 2013–2016 project added two floors.
buildings.address: Freret St at Newcomb Pl, New Orleans, LA 70118

buildings.name: McAlister Auditorium
buildings.description: Built in 1940, this Moderne take on the Roman Pantheon has a saucer-shaped, self-supporting concrete dome 110 feet (34 m) across, said at the time to be the largest of its kind in the world.

buildings.name: Devlin Fieldhouse
buildings.description: Paid for with the football team's earnings from the 1932 Rose Bowl, the 'Rose Bowl Gym' opened in 1933. It is still home to Green Wave basketball, with about 4,100 seats.

buildings.name: Yulman Stadium
buildings.description: Opened in 2014, Yulman Stadium brought Green Wave football back to campus for the first time since old Tulane Stadium was torn down in 1980. It seats 30,000 and was built so it can grow later.
buildings.architect: Gould Evans & Associates; Lee Ledbetter & Associates
buildings.address: 2900 Ben Weiner Dr, New Orleans, LA 70118

buildings.name: Newcomb Art Museum
buildings.description: The museum's galleries in the Woldenberg Art Center opened with a 1996 expansion of the Newcomb art department. It is known for its Newcomb Pottery, and two Tiffany stained-glass triptychs line its Woodward Way breezeway.
buildings.address: Woldenberg Art Center, Newcomb Pl, New Orleans, LA 70118

traditions.name: Don't Step on the Seal
traditions.description: Campus legend says that stepping on the university seal under Brookings Hall will keep you from graduating, though touching the Chancellor's Medallion breaks the curse. Find the seal and walk around it.

traditions.name: Declaration of Independence in Olin
traditions.description: Olin Library displays a broadside copy of the Declaration of Independence, printed before the document was signed to spread the news across the colonies. Stop by the exhibit to see it in person.

traditions.name: Lunch at Holmes Lounge
traditions.description: The old library reading room in Ridgley Hall is now Holmes Lounge, one of the most beautiful rooms on campus. Grab lunch there and take in the surroundings.

traditions.name: The Painted Underpass
traditions.description: The underpass linking the South 40 to the main campus is covered in painted announcements for campus events. Walk through to see the latest designs.

traditions.name: Assembly Series in Graham Chapel
traditions.description: Graham Chapel hosts the Assembly Series, the university's long-running lecture program, which has brought speakers such as Eleanor Roosevelt and Gloria Steinem to campus. Check the schedule and catch a talk.

details.airportInfo: Lambert is about 23 km northwest of downtown St. Louis. MetroLink's Red Line stops at both airport terminals.
details.funFact: Brookings Hall was the administration building of the 1904 World's Fair, and Francis Field on campus was the main stadium of the 1904 Summer Olympics, the first held in the Western Hemisphere.
details.languageInfo: The school colors are red and green, and the teams are the Bears, with a mascot named Forest the bear.
details.transportationFact: A free Campus Circulator shuttle loops the Danforth Campus, and MetroLink Blue Line trains stop at Skinker station beside it.

buildings.name: Brookings Hall
buildings.description: Cope and Stewardson designed this Collegiate Gothic gateway, built from 1900 to 1902 as the centerpiece of the new campus. It served as the administration building of the 1904 World's Fair and is still the university's administrative center.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.wiki: Washington University Hilltop Campus Historic District
buildings.name: Graham Chapel
buildings.description: Dedicated in 1909, this Collegiate Gothic chapel was modeled after King's College Chapel at Cambridge, though on a far smaller scale. It hosts concerts, plays and the university's Assembly Series lectures.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.wiki: Washington University Hilltop Campus Historic District
buildings.name: Busch Hall
buildings.description: Named for Anheuser-Busch co-founder Adolphus Busch, this was the first building begun on the campus, with its cornerstone laid in 1900. It was the chemistry building until 1950 and now houses humanities departments.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.wiki: Washington University Hilltop Campus Historic District
buildings.name: Ridgley Hall
buildings.description: The university's first library until the early 1960s, Ridgley displayed Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee gifts during the 1904 World's Fair. Its old reading room is now the ornate Holmes Lounge.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.wiki: Washington University Hilltop Campus Historic District
buildings.name: Eads Hall
buildings.description: In 1922, physics professor Arthur Holly Compton ran experiments in this hall's basement showing that light behaves as particles, work that won him the 1927 Nobel Prize. During the 1904 World's Fair it was used by the Board of Lady Managers.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.name: Olin Library
buildings.description: Dedicated in 1962 and renovated in 2003, Olin is the main library of the university and the largest library in Missouri. It holds a broadside of the Declaration of Independence printed before the signing.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.name: Steinberg Hall
buildings.description: Completed in 1960, this was the first commission of Fumihiko Maki, who later won the Pritzker Prize. It houses the Art and Architecture Library and the Department of Art History and Archaeology.
buildings.address: Danforth Campus, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130

buildings.name: Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum
buildings.description: Founded in 1881 as the oldest art museum west of the Mississippi, the museum moved into this Fumihiko Maki building in 2006. A 2019 renovation added a polished stainless steel facade and a sculpture garden.

buildings.name: Francis Olympic Field
buildings.description: Built for the 1904 World's Fair, this stadium was the main venue of the 1904 Summer Olympics, and its permanent stands were an early use of reinforced concrete. It is still home to the Bears' football, soccer and track teams.
buildings.address: Forsyth Blvd, St. Louis County, MO 63105

buildings.name: Francis Gymnasium
buildings.description: Built in 1903, this gym was the main indoor venue of the 1904 Summer Olympics, hosting boxing and fencing. It has been used by the university's athletics department ever since.
buildings.address: Forsyth Blvd, St. Louis County, MO 63105
